payload.text: The more than 1,900 startups on the The Crunchbase Unicorn Board have a combined valuation of roughly $9 trillion, based on their last reported valuations. But Crunchbase’s new Current Valuation Model , which estimates how private-company values have changed since their last funding rounds, puts that figure closer to $11 trillion. Most unicorns are estimated to have gained value, even as others have lost ground, our analysis shows. Among the biggest potential gainers are AI startups Thinking Machines Lab , whose estimated value has climbed from $12 billion to $40 billion, and Sierra , from nearly $16 billion to $31.5 billion. The majority of companies on the board are valued higher by the Current Valuations model than they were when they last raised funding. Only around 236 companies — roughly 12% of the board — are down by more than $100 million in value compared to their last reported valuations. The valuation model estimates that a select group of 24 companies have gained more than $10 billion in value since their most recent funding rounds. They include Mira Murati ’s AI research lab Thinking Machines Lab, which was last valued at $12 billion in its 2025 seed funding but has a current valuation projected at $40 billion. Similarly, Bret Taylor ’s customer oriented AI agent builder Sierra was last valued at close to $16  billion in a May 2026 funding round. It is now estimated to be valued at $31.5 billion, per the Crunchbase model. (On Monday, Bloomberg reported that Sierra is raising a new round at a roughly $30 billion valuation.) Physical Intelligence , a company building AI for robotics, was valued at $5.6 billion in its Series B. Crunchbase’s Current Valuation model estimates its valuation now at $18.5 billion. Another 53 companies are estimated to have current valuations that are $5 billion to just under $10 billion higher than those achieved in their most recent funding rounds. They include Unconventional AI , which is focused on energy efficiency for AI; Lila Sciences , which is building artificial intelligence for science; AI cloud company Vultr ; AI research lab humans& ; stablecoin payment platform Tempo ; and Yann LeCun ’s Advanced Machine Intelligence , which is modeling physical world intelligence. A total of 484 companies are estimated to have current valuations that are $1 billion to $5 billion higher than their most recent funding valuations. More than 1,100 companies have values that were flat or up to $1 billion higher than their most recent funding valuations. Only around 236 companies are estimated to be below their most recent valuation, by more than $100 million. Collectively, their current valuations are down by $326 billion from their most recent fundings, Crunchbase estimates. Unicorn growth The Crunchbase Unicorn Board reached its highest value in 2026 as three companies approached or exceeded $1 trillion valuations — unprecedented in the board’s history. The board peaked at $10 trillion in advance of the Anthropic IPO this past week. The company’s public-market debut removed close to $1 trillion from the board. This followed another trillion-dollar exit from the board earlier this year, when SpaceX — last valued at $1.3 trillion in a secondary financing this year — before it went public in June at a value of $1.8 trillion. All told, the unicorn board this year is currently up by $1.5 trillion from its $7.5 trillion value at the end of 2025. With its closest rival now on the public markets, OpenAI is currently the most highly valued private company at an official valuation of $1.25 trillion. The unicorn board has picked up pace this year. Around 360 companies joined the board so far this year, the second highest count in a single year after 2021 when 621 companies joined. A faster pace of new entrants and rising valuations have helped replenish the board, while current estimates suggest substantial additional value has accumulated between funding rounds. The next test is how closely these estimated values align with prices investors are willing to pay. Future funding rounds, secondary transactions, public listings and M&A will reveal how much of the board’s estimated $2 trillion uplift translates into realized value. Further reading: The Crunchbase Unicorn Board Methodology Current valuations are based on the new Crunchbase Current Valuation Model , which prices companies using a proprietary machine learning model that starts with a company’s most recent post-money valuation and continuously estimates how its value has shifted since that funding event. The model covers roughly 230,000 funded private companies. Read more here . Illustration: Dom Guzman

Galvanize Therapeutics , $130M, biotech : Redwood City, California-based Galvanize Therapeutics, a developer of pulsed electric field ablation technologies for oncology and chronic disease, picked up $130 million in Series D funding led by HealthQuest Capital . 4. Marrow Therapeutics , $120M, biotech : Watertown, Massachusetts-based Marrow Therapeutics, a developer of bone marrow-targeted therapies to treat severe blood disorders, announced its launch with a combined $173 million in Series A and B funding. Orbimed led its $120 million Series B round while Scion Life Sciences and venBio led the $53 million Series A. 7. Noeri , $110M, enterprise AI : Noeri, a developer of self-improving AI for enterprises and researchers, launched with $110 million in initial funding. Menlo Ventures led the round for the Palo Alto-based startup, which was founded by Stanford University computer science professors. 8. payload.text: This is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar. Check out our previous entry here . What if solar farms could keep generating electricity after sunset with a little help from mirrors orbiting Earth? Or researchers could send an experiment into space for less than the price of a car? Those are two of the more unusual ideas that attracted startup investment in the past month. Our latest roundup also includes a company bringing AI to the old-school business of garbage hauling, another rethinking how factories are programmed, and a consumer brand betting that better breathing could become a big business. Let’s take a closer look. $73.5M to reflect sunlight from space Solar power has one rather obvious limitation: The sun goes down. To that end, Reflect Orbital is working on a solution that sounds straight out of science fiction. The Hawthorne, California-based startup wants to put giant mirrors in orbit to redirect sunlight toward specific locations on Earth, potentially allowing solar farms to keep generating electricity longer after sunset. The company recently announced $73.5 million in new funding , bringing its total funding to more than $102 million, per Crunchbase . Existing investors Sequoia Capital , Lux Capital and Starship Ventures participated, alongside new backers including Buckley Ventures , Convective Capital , The Uncommon Group and Salesforce Ventures 1 . Reflect Orbital is developing lightweight, foldable reflectors that it says can be launched aboard satellites and deployed in low Earth orbit. The company envisions using them not only to extend solar power generation, but also to illuminate disaster zones for nighttime search-and-rescue operations or construction sites after dark. The idea remains unproven in orbit, however. Reflect Orbital is targeting the second quarter of 2027 for its first demonstration mission, which has received FCC approval. The funding will help support those initial launches, further development of its reflector technology, and commercial partnerships. The raise comes during a record year for space technology funding. By late August, investors had poured $20.3 billion into space- and satellite-related startups globally , per Crunchbase data, already comfortably exceeding previous annual records. Related Crunchbase queries: Space And Satellite Tech Startup Funding Global Cleantech Startup Funding In 2026 $62M to make better breathing a bigger business Nasal strips have been around for decades, but Intake Breathing Technology thinks there’s room for a serious upgrade. The Santa Barbara, California-based consumer wellness company recently announced a $62 million investment from Camino Partners , the investment platform founded by KIND Snacks entrepreneur Daniel Lubetzky . Intake makes a patented magnetic nasal dilator designed to open nasal passages and improve airflow. Rather than relying on a conventional adhesive strip stretched across the nose, its system uses adhesive tabs and a reusable magnetic band to pull the sides of the nose outward. The company markets its product to people looking to breathe more comfortably while sleeping, exercising or going about their daily routines. It says it has sold more than 100 million pairs of breathing tabs since 2023, with triple-digit revenue growth over the past three years. Intake plans to use the new capital to expand beyond its direct-to-consumer business and into more mainstream retail channels. That’s where Lubetzky’s experience building KIND into a household name could prove useful. Its funding comes as venture investors show renewed enthusiasm for fitness and wellness. Startups in those categories raised more than $3.6 billion globally in the first half of 2026 , putting the sector on pace for its strongest funding year since 2022, Crunchbase data shows. Interestingly, much of this year’s investment into the sector has flowed to wearable devices and health platforms built around AI and data. Intake is a somewhat different bet: a relatively simple physical product that has apparently found a sizable audience without promising to reinvent healthcare through software. Related Crunchbase query: Global Fitness- And Wellness-Related Startup Funding In 2026 $12M to bring AI to the garbage-hauling business Taking out the trash isn’t exactly rocket science. But managing the businesses that collect it turns out to be surprisingly complicated. San Francisco-based TrashLab Software recently raised $12 million in a growth funding round led by Ventana , with participation from existing investors Bienville Capital , Harlem Capital and CreativeCo . The startup builds an AI-powered operating platform for waste-hauling businesses, an industry where many smaller operators still rely on spreadsheets, paper routes and clunky software to manage their fleets. TrashLab says its platform combines dispatching, route planning, customer management, billing and payments. Its AI agent, called Haul-E, can answer customer calls and take orders, while cameras in garbage trucks can help document problems such as overflowing dumpsters, blocked containers or bins that weren’t put out for collection. The company says hundreds of waste haulers across the U.S. and Canada now use its software, and that more than 5 million tons of material have been managed through its platform. It’s not the only startup finding an AI opportunity in the waste industry. We recently covered Greyparrot , a London-based company using computer vision to identify and analyze waste moving through recycling facilities. While Greyparrot focuses on what happens after trash reaches a processing plant, TrashLab is tackling the messy logistics of getting it there. Related Crunchbase query: Global Venture Funding To Waste Management Startups In 2026 $10M to let engineers program factories in plain English Factory automation has come a long way, but programming the machines that run industrial production lines can still require specialized expertise and a lot of time. Gardena, California-based Neuron Industries wants to make the process a lot simpler. The startup recently announced a $10 million seed round co-led by FCVC and Obvious Ventures , with participation from Y Combinator , Thin Line Capital , Zee Prime Capital and Founder Factor . Neuron is developing a new kind of industrial controller — the hardware that coordinates sensors, motors and other equipment in factories — alongside AI-powered software that lets engineers describe what they want a machine to do in ordinary language. Its system generates control code that engineers can inspect, modify and test in simulation before deploying it to real equipment. The goal is to reduce the time and specialized programming knowledge needed to get new production lines up and running. The startup says it has already demonstrated its technology on existing factory equipment, including replacing an aging controller on a wood-processing line with roughly three hours of engineering work and eight hours of downtime. It plans to release its Cortex AI Controller commercially in early 2027. The investment fits into a broader surge in funding for physical AI — technology that applies artificial intelligence to robots, autonomous vehicles, industrial equipment and other machines in the real world. Startups in those categories raised $47.4 billion globally across 521 deals in the first half of 2026 , nearly 4x the amount invested in the second half of 2025, according to Crunchbase data. Related Crunchbase query: Global Physical AI Venture Funding In 2026 €6.9M to make space experiments more affordable Sending an experiment into space has traditionally required years of preparation, specialized engineering expertise and a very substantial budget. Austria-based Tumbleweed wants to bring the cost of entry down to as little as 15,000 euros. The Vienna startup recently raised 6.9 million euros (roughly $8 million) in seed funding led by PactVC , with participation from Vanagon Ventures , Prototype Capital and EWOR , among other investors. The company describes it as the largest space-tech seed round raised in Austria to date. Tumbleweed develops standardized containers, called Pods, that allow researchers and companies to conduct experiments in microgravity without building their own satellites or navigating the complex certification process required for space missions. Customers can place their experiments inside the pre-certified containers, which provide power and communications capabilities while in orbit. The startup handles the logistics of launching the payloads and transmitting experimental data back to Earth. Unlike many space startups still working toward their first launch, Tumbleweed has already put hardware in orbit. Its inaugural Oasis Alpha satellite launched in July carrying experiments for four paying customers, including research into biological processes and space-resource technologies. The mission was fully booked a year before launch. Tumbleweed says its new funding will help it carry out three more missions in 2027 and develop a next-generation spacecraft that would allow customers to bring physical samples back to Earth beginning in 2028. Tumbleweed is part of a growing European space startup ecosystem, although funding remains concentrated elsewhere. As of late August, European companies had attracted about 10% of global space-tech venture investment in 2026 , compared with the more than 60% going to U.S. startups, Crunchbase data shows. payload.text: By David Spreng The financing of the AI buildout is shifting from equity to debt, and those who invested through the telecom bubble may recognize what that shift tends to mean. There is an old story in Stephen Hawking ’s “A Brief History of Time” about a scientist lecturing on the universe when a woman in the audience insists that the world rests on the back of a giant turtle. Asked what the turtle stands on, she replies that it’s “turtles all the way down.” Her response is what philosophers call infinite regress — a chain of claims in which each one rests on another of the same kind and solid ground never arrives. David Spreng is the founder, co-CEO and co-CIO of Runway Growth Capital. I think of it when I look at the AI buildout because its logic has taken the same shape. Valuations support borrowing, and borrowing builds capacity. The capacity then becomes proof that the valuations were right, so each claim stands on the one beneath it. Over the past year, more of the stack has started running on debt rather than equity, and in my experience, that crossing is the moment the telecom bubble becomes the relevant history given that debt may change how these stories end. Until recently, the AI buildout was largely an equity-financed story, with venture investment reaching record levels. Crunchbase data shows global venture funding totaled $679 billion through the first three quarters of 2026, the highest amount ever recorded for that period. AI companies attracted $102 billion in the third quarter alone, accounting for roughly 64% of global venture funding. A record 27 companies raised rounds of $1 billion or more during the quarter, collectively accounting for about a third of that total. Equity financing carries significant risks, but unlike debt, it generally does not impose fixed repayment obligations. When investments underperform, equity investors typically absorb losses through declining valuations, while companies may retain greater flexibility to pursue their long-term strategies. That debt is now arriving in size. Meta sold $30 billion of bonds last October in one of the largest corporate debt sales on record , then returned for $25 billion more in April , with investors reportedly demanding more compensation the second time. Amazon , Alphabet and Oracle have each borrowed tens of billions of their own , and Meta’s giant Louisiana data-center campus was financed with a record $27 billion bond raised by a joint-venture partner rather than by Meta itself. Morgan Stanley expects the big AI and cloud companies to spend about $3 trillion on infrastructure through 2028, with only about half of it expected to come from their own cash flow. The rest has to come from somewhere, and increasingly I think that somewhere is the bond market and private credit. I watched the earlier version of this from a front-row seat, first as a venture capitalist in the late 1990s and since then as a lender to growth-stage technology companies. Telecom borrowed staggering sums against a demand forecast that was widely repeated and rarely checked, the famous claim that internet traffic was doubling every 100 days . Traffic was actually doubling about once a year, spectacular growth but a fraction of what the borrowing assumed. By 2002 the telecom sector carried roughly $1 trillion in debt , much of which the chairman of the FCC told Congress would never be repaid, and WorldCom had entered what was then the largest bankruptcy in American history . Much of the fiber the industry laid sat dark for years and was finally put to work by buyers who paid pennies on the dollar for it in bankruptcy, through a decade of restructurings and private mergers that rebuilt entire cap tables. Some companies survived that process, and many did not. The demand narrative The echo that concerns me most is the demand narrative. Today’s version holds that data centers are effectively leased before they are built and that the only real mistake is building too little. That may prove correct, but it is repeated with the same uniformity the traffic forecast enjoyed in 1999, and much of it rests on projections supplied by the companies doing the building. What has changed in recent months is that investors have begun demanding an answer. Anthropic is now public, and once companies of that scale report financial results every quarter, investors can check the demand story against audited numbers. Some may argue, reasonably, that my comparison fails and that the companies doing the largest borrowing may be among the most profitable enterprises ever built, with cash flows the telecom carriers never approached. A few AI companies also appear to be reaching revenue scale faster than any businesses before them. And the internet really did change everything, just as the traffic really did arrive. All of that may be true, and none of it answers the question I think a lender has to ask, which is whether the cash arrives on the schedule the debt requires. Equity can generally wait out a wrong timeline in a way debt cannot, and when borrowed money builds capacity faster than revenue arrives to service it, in my opinion, the correction tends to come through restructurings rather than quiet markdowns. Enduring lessons None of this is a prediction that the AI buildout must end the way telecom did. The most durable lesson of the telecom bust, in my view, concerned capital structure, which decided who was still standing when demand finally caught up with capacity, long after the technology itself had been vindicated. I have spent years arguing that growth companies fear debt more than they should , and I still believe it, but the argument has always been conditional. Debt serves borrowers whose obligations are sized to revenue they can see and lenders who underwrite fundamentals instead of narratives, and it treats everyone else harshly. I believe the borrowing stacked beneath the AI boom will be judged by that standard. Every assumption in the stack may well hold, but what I learned the last time is that once investors begin asking what the turtles are standing on, they rarely stop until they reach something solid. David Spreng is the founder, co-CEO and co-CIO of Runway Growth Capital . He has more than 30 years of experience as a Silicon Valley venture capitalist and growth debt lender, has been involved in the formation and development of nearly 50 technology companies, and has appeared four times on the Forbes Midas List of top venture capitalists. He co-founded Decathlon Capital Partners in 2010, served on the board of the National Venture Capital Association and has participated as a panelist at the World Economic Forum in Davos. payload.text: By Alberto Onetti The “blue economy,” which encompasses industries built around oceans and coasts — from shipping and fisheries to offshore energy and marine biotechnology — is one of the largest, yet least visible, engines of the global economy. For startups, that means opportunities to modernize how we move goods, produce energy and manage marine resources. Alberto Onetti, Mind The Bridge The blue economy has doubled in size in just a quarter of a century, reaching $2.6 trillion in value. To put this in perspective: If the blue economy were a country, it would be the world’s fifth largest. And as the world turns back to the sea to face increasingly critical challenges, from geopolitical instability to rising energy prices and climate resilience, the blue economy is set to become even more central. Powerful “blue technology” forces of disruption are at play. Digitalization and automation, the energy transition, environmental pressures and advances in marine biotechnology are all reshaping how value is created at sea. Investment in those technologies is also accelerating, with an emphasis on sustainable development. Blue tech companies tracked in Mind the Bridge ’s “Rethinking the Blue Economy” report, produced with support from Crunchbase, raised almost $10 billion through the third quarter of 2026 — already exceeding the $6.2 billion raised in all of 2025. Large rounds for defense companies with maritime applications account for much of that surge. Blue tech: A sector defying global slowdown Against the prevailing trend in the global innovation landscape, blue tech has followed a substantially continuous upward trajectory since 2021, producing an average of 70 new scaleups per year — even more rapidly over the past two years. Preliminary figures for 2026 suggest that roughly 100 new blue tech scaleups may emerge by year-end. The same trend is evident in funding figures. In 2025, blue tech funding has reached $6.2 billion, double than the previous year. As of Q3 2026, blue tech scaleups worldwide had already raised almost $10 billion in new capital. If this trend continues, we expect the sector to attract more than $12 billion by year-end. The drivers? Exceptional maritime resilience deals involving defense and infrastructure companies such as Anduril Industries ($5 billion raised in 2026) and Helsing ($1.8 billion raised in 2026). Not all blue tech is the same Blue tech is a broad category including a diverse set of technologies, some of which are more mature than others. To shed light on the sector’s composition, we clustered each unique technology developed by blue tech scaleups into 20 groups. We then assessed each group from two different perspectives: impact on the industry and market commitment (a combination of scaleup and capital invested density). The result is a matrix highlighting: Transformational technologies that have a high impact and are relatively well-established. Among those, AI and machine learning, and robotics and industrial automation occupies a particular sweet spot of high impact, substantial investment and high scaleup density (more than 200 scaleups and $20 billion invested in total). High-potential disruptive technologies, with only relatively lower levels of investment and scaleup density (roughly 50 scaleups and $3 billion to $5 billion invested per cluster). Among them, the most promising ones are maritime clean propulsion and sustainable fuels, and supply chain and freight tech. The other quadrants are populated by transversal technologies with a more indirect impact on the industry and emerging niche technologies. Ports: the ‘smartest smart cities’ The ultimate question is: Who will ride the wave of change of the Blue Economy? Short answer: ports. Ports are where the dynamics reshaping maritime activities converge most visibly, acting as mini “blue economies.” In many ways, ports are the “smartest smart cities” — dense, complex systems where energy, logistics, data, mobility and people meet. They are places where innovation can be tested at scale before spreading to the wider economy. And like smart cities a decade ago, they now need a playbook. To provide a comprehensive perspective from the ports’ point of view, in our report we interviewed 10 of the world’s leading port authorities to understand their priorities, challenges and barriers to innovation. While doing so, we collected several case studies from authorities such as the ports of Barcelona, Bergen, Seattle, Rotterdam and Los Angeles — true blueprints of best practices in tackling the innovation challenges of the blue economy. The result is a picture that shows the potential of blue tech as the catalyst for a radical evolution of one of the largest sectors of the global economy. To “ride the wave,” most ports are already activating multiple open innovation tools — some with a structured approach and dedicated units. Yet, to really “get there” port authorities, operators, startups, investors and policymakers need a shared agenda and vision, working on the same challenges. Early but substantial efforts are already underway. A prime example is BlueTechPort by the Port of Barcelona , a collaborative innovation hub connecting entrepreneurs, technology providers, researchers and maritime businesses. The initiative, detailed in a full case study available in the report, is already expanding internationally through the Lighthouse International Acceleration Program, powered by Mind the Bridge . Notice to (innovation) sailors: the course of blue economy innovation is set. The challenge now is to catch the favorable winds — and ride them. Get the full story in Mind The Bridge’s report, available for free download here . Alberto Onetti is chairman of Mind the Bridge and a professor at University of Insubria . He is a serial entrepreneur who has started three startups in his career, the last of which is Funambol , among the five Italian scaleups that have raised the largest amount of capital. He is recognized among the leading international experts in open innovation and has wide experience in setting up and managing open innovation projects — venture clients, venture builders, intrapreneurship, CVCs — with large multinational companies, as well as advising and training on this subject. Onetti has a column on Sifted ( Financial Times ) and several other tech blogs.

payload.text: AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines. But even so, investors haven’t lost interest in startups focused on finding, filling and managing jobs for actual humans. So far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data shows. Not surprisingly, the vast majority are also incorporating a heavy dose of AI. To get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years. Broadly, findings show 2026 funding on track to meet or slightly exceed year-ago levels, albeit with reduced deal count. Top fundraisers Much of this year’s investment has gone to a small group of companies. To illustrate, below we put together a list of 14 of the largest fundraisers. As you can see, it’s a varied list, with a commonly shared theme of bringing more automation to hiring, HR and payroll tasks. By far the largest funding recipient is Mercor , a startup that pairs human experts with developers of AI models and tools. The 4-year-old company raised $750 million in a Series D round this month at a whopping $20 billion valuation. San Francisco-based Mercor is betting that as companies build AI agents to take on more work tasks, demand for subject matter experts to guide these efforts will grow. While frontier labs have been its primary buyers for the past few years, Mercor says it expects enterprises will soon be its major customers. The next two largest fundraisers on our list for this year are focused on automating more employer tasks. Paris-based Skello secured $220 million this summer for its AI-enabled software platform for HR teams. And HiBob , a New York-based platform for HR and payroll, picked up $166 million in a Salesforce 1 -led financing. Startups focused on jobseekers Of course, investors aren’t only looking at startups automating work tasks or training AI agents to do so. They’re also backing companies focused on the old-fashioned business of matching workers and employers. In this sector, one of the larger rounds this year went to San Francisco-based Juicebox , an AI tool for recruiters to find talented candidates. The 4-year-old company picked up an $80 million Series B at an $850 million valuation. Agentic hiring is also a thing. Metaview , a San Francisco-based startup that offers an agentic recruiting platform optimized, in its words, to “get the right butts in seats,” secured $60 million in a September Series C financing. Around the same time, London’s Jack & Jill AI , which offers AI agents for finding careers and for hiring, closed on $40 million in Series A funding. Another agentic hiring platform, San Francisco’s Paraform , announced a $40 million round this spring, pitching itself as an offering for an age in which employers are making fewer hires overall but still need highly skilled people for highly paid jobs. Surprisingly depressing So what kind of employment future do startup funding trends paint for human jobseekers? Not a good one. As a human who has spent decades writing about sector-specific startup funding, this is probably the most depressing data dive into investment trends for an industry that I have ever done. Overall, the bulk of big rounds are going to one of three categories: using humans to help train their potential AI replacements, automating work tasks around supporting people in the workplace, and getting AI to help hire the right people for the dwindling pool of available positions. Typically, I’m rooting for startups to succeed. And honestly, there’s not an individual company highlighted here that I’m specifically hoping will fail. But nonetheless, the broad vision of an increasingly AI-dominated workplace does bring with it a sense of trepidation. title: Public Markets Are Frequently Wrong. The SaaSpocalypse Shows Us Why

payload.text: By Richard Anton Panics and pile-ons are a familiar pattern in the public markets, with a herd mentality wiping value from companies in an instant. Trading can swiftly become a barometer of emotions, rather than a well-informed gauge of value. We have seen this play out with AI’s impact on software companies and the supposed end of the Software as a Service business model. The doom-laden talk of the SaaSpocalypse was noise, with little signal, and most traders were initially unable to distinguish between a company that will thrive in the AI age and one that will be decimated by it. The SaaSpocalypse didn’t reveal the end of software. It revealed the limits of public markets in judging its value. This pattern erodes trust in the public markets. For companies, being publicly owned may no longer be appealing, and founders considering an exit may not view an initial public offering as the ultimate goal. How the markets got it wrong Richard Anton, co-founder and general partner of Oxx. The markets have struggled to keep up with the tech advances of the AI era and judge their impact on incumbent companies. Sometimes they underreacted and ignored these developments, and other times they overreacted and panicked. When OpenAI launched ChatGPT to the public in November 2022, Alphabet stock was punished even though later Google emerged as a clear winner with generative AI. And with SaaS, the markets were slow to respond to the advent of generative and agentic AI through to the end of 2025. The market capitalization of enterprise software companies continued to rise through this period, until January 2026 when all hell broke loose. The launch of Claude Cowork triggered a panic, especially when additional plug-ins were announced later that month that targeted specific workflows for enterprise support functions such as HR and legal. From there, valuations went into a tailspin, with traders treating software companies indiscriminately. Over two days, an estimated $285 billion of market capitalization was wiped from software, data analytics and financial tech companies, and by April the benchmark cloud software index — the BVP Nasdaq Emerging Cloud Index —  had dropped by 31% since the start of the year. As an investor in software over many decades, I have seen this pattern many times before. AI does not mean the end of software companies. Rather, AI has driven a shift in how software is built, where user growth will come from — primarily agents rather than humans — and in the sources of defensible competitive advantage. This was always going to benefit some companies, like those deeply embedded into their customers’ core business processes, and harm others. The recovery has been uneven and markets still get it wrong There were predictions of the death of SaaS, but this is the hype cycle pattern that always plays out when new technology emerges: a surge of excitement, then a correction, then productivity. In the short term, the markets overestimated the harm AI would inflict on the software sector as a whole. That is now being corrected as the markets start to realize which companies benefit from AI and which are threatened by it. At the end of October, the cloud software index was up by 26% since the start of the year and by a massive 83% since its nadir in April. At my firm, Oxx , we never believed in the SaaSpocalypse, and the markets have recovered from this turmoil. The recovery is bifurcated with some sub sectors, like cybersecurity and data and analytics, faring well while others, like workflow management, have fallen back. In cybersecurity, a great example is CrowdStrike , whose share price dropped by 27% in early 2026 but was up 114% between the start of the year and the end of October. The problem with public markets is part of a bigger trend The knee-jerk reactions to the latest developments with AI, however, are not just temporary market sentiment. They are part of a broader shift that has occurred since the late 1990s and accelerated in 2002 when the Sarbanes-Oxley Act was introduced to improve investor protections in the wake of the dot com crash. It produced the unintended consequence of driving company ownership from public to private markets. While the number of public companies in the U.S. has halved, private markets have grown dramatically in recent years. This is where much of the smart money can be found, along with a more accurate, and patient, assessment of software companies’ value. The panic over the SaaSpocalypse has shown that the public markets aren’t an accurate reflection of the intrinsic value of many software companies. This disconnect may be causing a systematic mispricing of private company transactions — multiple transactions which had been in process early this year fell away in the wake of the false signals which came from public markets. This needs to be addressed. At the moment, few people recognize there’s a problem with the pricing function of public markets, and the first step to solving this issue is to recognize there is actually a problem. Richard Anton is the co-founder and general partner of Oxx , a specialist software investor backing European founders on a mission to transform their industries with AI at the moment they’re readying to scale. Anthropic priced shares for its upcoming stock market debut at $83 on Wednesday evening, solidly above the expected range of $70 to $78 laid out in its IPO filing. The offering promised to be the public market event of the season, with the Claude creator seeing investor demand for shares well in excess of its capital-raising goals. The stock is trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic is selling 980 million shares, including 23.6 million from selling shareholders, up from it’s earlier plan to sell just over 800 million shares. At that upgraded size, the offering is bringing in around $80 billion for the company. Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD , Broadcom , Google , Micron Technology , Microsoft , Nvidia and TSMC . Put together, the IPO and private placement total around $106 billion. It’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut. SpaceX , by comparison, raised $86 billion in its June offering. Fast growth but no profits, yet The IPO follows a revenue growth trajectory for the history books. For the first nine months of the year, the company had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. Anthropic claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology to date, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026. As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago. payload.text: Anthropic starts trading on the Nasdaq tomorrow with a growth story that’s unlike any I’ve seen in close to three decades working in Silicon Valley: The company says revenue reached $17 billion in Q3, less than four years after Claude launched with zero. The San Francisco-based company also presents a stark contrast to the more common theme in recent years of venture-backed companies staying private longer: Anthropic is less than six years old as it goes public in a potentially record-setting listing. Those metrics are impressive, but there are other numbers in its S-1 I keep circling, too, like the nearly $900 billion in compute purchase and lease commitments. I’ve worked in Silicon Valley through the dot-com boom and bust, the rise of SaaS, social media, unicorn and decacorn startups and now, AI. Anthropic’s extraordinary rise and entrance onto the public markets marks a new technology era — one with enormous growth and potential, but also tremendous costs, risks and unknowns. OpenAI ’s seminal success was the launch of chatbots in 2022 — within two months, ChatGPT reached 100 million users and in less than four years, OpenAI had a billion monthly active users. By contrast, Anthropic’s breakout was the success of Claude Code, launched just last year. Already, Anthropic says 11,900 companies use the product, spending $100,000 or more trailing 12 months, up 12x from a year ago. In its S-1 , the company says that marks the fastest enterprise adoption for any company on record. Anthropic’s IPO could value it at $1.4 trillion and raise $88.5 billion via the IPO and concurrent private placement. As it becomes public, I’ll be watching closely to see if the company can keep turning demand for Claude and Claude Code into a durable business while building out the astounding amount of compute it says it needs and managing the many risks that surround its technology. By the numbers Here are some of the other key details and figures that caught my eye ahead of Anthropic’s first day on the public markets: The company has a purchase and lease agreement for $895.4 billion for compute. Of that, $447.5 billion will be incurred before the end of 2030. Anthropic currently has over $100 billion on its balance sheet. Its IPO seeks to add another roughly $100 billion, creating a war chest for those compute commitments. When it launched Claude in the first quarter of 2023, Anthropic had zero revenue. In less than four years, revenue reached $17 billion in Q3 2026, up 12x from Q3 2025. More than 1,900 customers spend more than $1 million and 250 more than $10 million, trailing 12 months, according to the company. Its per-employee revenue figures are impressive: Each employee supports $6.6 million in trailing 12-month revenue as of Sept 30, 2026. Anthropic is putting aside 5% of equity for a fund devoted to public good, adding 2% for every 50% increase in share price. Each founder is selling roughly $250 million worth of shares in the listing, depending on its final listing price. The backers behind Anthropic’s rise Anthropic got to where it is now through a fast sequence of funding rounds, from its Jaan Tallinn -led Series A in 2021 to its Series H in May of this year that valued the company at $965 billion. Other lead investors over its many funding rounds include Google , Amazon , Spark Capital , Menlo Ventures , Lightspeed Venture Partners , Coatue and Sequoia Capital, all of whom are slated to be among the winners when it goes public tomorrow. Risks, opportunities and what’s ahead The AI era has the potential to generate massive amounts of new wealth and unlock life-changing technological advances. But it also comes with huge risks. Anthropic’s S-1 captures that tension. The opportunity the company describes extends far beyond coding and software. It says its focus in 2027 will be AI agents for knowledge work and scientific discovery. It also points to potential gains in biology and rare-disease research, economic growth, wider access to health care and improved government services. The S-1 cites the World Health Organization ’s estimate that 4.6 billion people lack access to basic health services. That promise comes with a competitive risk for its customers, too: Companies may worry that data they share with AI providers could help train models that compete with their products, or that more capable models could erode parts of their existing businesses. Anthropic’s S-1 also flags risks ranging from cyber and biological attacks to unpredictable model behavior, authoritarian surveillance and economic disruption. Anthropic’s public-benefit structure is meant to balance those competing pressures. As a public benefit corporation, the company says it must weigh commercial success against the public good. Its founders, employees and Long-Term Benefit Trust share in governance; the trust has no financial stake and weighs impacts on national security, economics, global health and science. Anthropic points to its launch of Mythos as an example of that balance. As Anthropic debuts tomorrow, I’ll be watching how well it balances AI’s promise with the risks its own filing lays out. payload.text: By Kenza Zayani In October, reports that OpenAI ‘s annualized revenue was running well below earlier estimates sent AI-linked stocks sharply lower and prompted a fresh round of scrutiny over AI valuations. It also reopened a question investors have been circling for a while: Is ARR still the right way to describe an AI business? The limitations have been understood for some time. ARR was built for software companies selling predictable annual contracts, which is only part of how most AI companies make money. Through the early part of the generative AI boom, growth was steep enough that few people pressed the point. The OpenAI episode has made it harder to leave alone, partly because it showed how much weight public markets now place on a single private company’s numbers. For founders, this is worth paying attention to now rather than later. A cohort of AI companies is reaching the growth-capital stage, and the questions they face in diligence are changing. What ARR was built for Kenza Zayani of RTP Global. ARR became standard in the mid- to late-2000s, when software moved from licence fees to recurring subscriptions. A customer signed for 12 months, revenue became predictable and annualizing it was arithmetic rather than forecasting. The first generation of post-ChatGPT companies inherited it without much examination, despite earning money in a different way. Most now run hybrid models: a subscription base with consumption charges on top, billed against API calls, tokens processed or compute used. A growing number charge per outcome. An annualized figure blends revenue a customer has committed to with revenue that depends on what they use next month. What gets presented as ARR is usually a revenue run rate: recent revenue multiplied out to an annual figure. That is a reasonable way to describe momentum, and a less reliable guide to the year ahead. The first question an investor tends to ask is what the figure actually counts. Companies that sell partly through partners can report either the full value of those sales or only the share they keep, and the two conventions produce very different numbers for the same business. Both are legitimate, but the two are not necessarily comparable. Take two companies both reporting a $10 million annualized run rate. In the first, most of that revenue is contracted, and comes from customers whose usage has expanded steadily over 12 months. In the second, it rests on a handful of customers whose consumption spiked in the last quarter. These are not similar businesses. The first has demonstrated that customers keep coming back and spending more. Nothing in the headline figure tells you that. Looking beyond the headline If a single figure cannot separate those two businesses, the question is what can. The answer depends on the stage. At pre-seed and seed, the number matters. A steep trajectory can point to market demand, to customers willing to pay, and to a team beginning to crack go-to-market. A run rate isn’t generally expected to predict the year at that size. Later you need more. What matters is the revenue behind the number: customer concentration, how much is contracted rather than consumed, how predictable that revenue is, and whether the gross margins hold as volume rises. Retention and expansion are the centerpiece. They tell you how essential a product has become and whether it will still be in use in a few years. Churn is diagnostic in a way a growth figure never is. It can point to demand the product is not answering, pricing that does not match the value, a need that was never really recurring, or a market shallower than it first looked. What investors will expect next ARR has been a staple of how high-growth tech companies demonstrate momentum for such a long time that it’s not likely to disappear anytime soon. What is changing is how much weight that single number can carry on its own. Expect more investors to ask what a figure actually counts, how much of it is committed revenue, and what retention looks like by cohort. The founders who have those answers ready will tell a much more convincing story than a single number ever could. Kenza Zayani is an early-stage investor at RTP Global , based in London. She is drawn to ambitious founders tackling the most challenging problems, with a particular interest in AI from infrastructure to applications. Zayani has built experience in venture capital across stages, and at RTP Global, she brings her multistage experience and data-driven approach to company building with founders. title: Assets
summary:
> *AI 扩展了我能够同时推进的任务数量，却没有等比例扩展我的注意力、记忆力和认知调节能力。*

# 累

眼酸、头皮紧、脑袋的中心明显靠前（感觉脑门比后脑勺重），坐电脑前两三个小时感觉比以前上一天班都累，应该不只我一个人有这种感受。

以前写代码的时候，可能连续几个小时只关注或者主要关注一个需求/bug，即便期间涉及和其他人的讨论、上网查资料、翻 stack overflow，并不是纯粹在 vs code 里看/写代码，但始终是在一个主线上，注意力是相对集中的。

但 2026 年以来，随着模型能力越来越强，好用的 Agent 越来越多，我使用 AI 的强度也随之增大，具体表现在数量飙升的 GitHub commits 和 pr，在非常短的时间里，经历了“掌握”多任务并发能力的从兴奋，到沉迷，再到疲惫的过程。

我可以同时让几个 Agent 做需求分析、技术调研、样式设计、功能实现，我需要做的就是下达指令、提供授权、验收成果和思考如何优化流程。

这期间的直观感受是工作推进很快，特别是几个 session 同时亮起小绿点时，那种即将逐个验收成果的期待感和盲目的满足感，和游戏里抽卡一样上头，那个时刻应该有很多多巴胺在分泌。

但结果通常不如人意，抽卡嘛，歪是常态，这个时候就得调整心态，看看哪儿不合适，重新写写提示词再抽一轮，然后换到另一个 session 里进行上述动作，有时候得想着将重复的劳动做成自动化或者沉淀为 skill，一边调教一边寻找优化 workflow 的空间。

一天的时间很快就过去了，沉浸式 vibe 的时候，时间的流速和打游戏的时候是一样的，但打游戏不累，打玛莲妮亚和杨戬死 10 次重新打我都不累，但 vibe coding 一天下来是真累。。。

# 注意力磨损/残留/负荷

起初我觉得是中间缺少休息了，比如 45 分钟课间休息 10 分钟或许会好一些，以及我可能不应该同时处理几个项目，毕竟我不是 MacBook 没有 10 个核，于是我开始尝试没 45 分钟起来走走，并且控制并发数在 3 个。但效果并不明显，还是同样很容易感到疲惫。

于是我咬咬牙，克制自己在等待模型响应时去处理其它任务的冲动，等的时候就想眼前的事情或者发呆，这半天就干一件事情，效果很显著，从 9:30 到 11:50，中间起来活动一次，头皮完全没有之前那种紧绷感，脑袋也很清明。坐在电脑前的时间是一样的，工作强度也差不多，只是将两个多小时的时间同时处理 3 件事变为处理一件事，就有明显的体感差异。

那么原因是什么？

午休的时候我就在琢磨这件事，偶然联想到打球，或许思考时的大脑就像运动时的身体，持续而稳定的负荷，相较于频繁启停变换，会造成额外的消耗，就像跑步和打羽毛球的区别。一个人同样的体力，跑步能坚持半个小时，但羽毛球或许十分钟就得歇一歇。

在羽毛球比赛中，业余和职业的体能差距很大，一部分原因就是职业运动员更善于采用经济的跑动步伐、合理的节奏和高效的回合间休息。那么类比多任务工作时的疲惫感，是不是因为我们在用一种很不经济的方式使用自己的大脑，或者更精确一点说是使用自己的注意力？

于是咨询了一下 GPT，简要描述了我的感受和猜想，让它分析问题的原因是否如我所想，并查查有没有类似的理论依据支撑。得到的答复很长，粗略翻一下估计得有八九页，核心观点是——**疲惫不一定来自能量被大量消耗，可能来自持续认知控制所付出的额外代价**。

理论依据引用了一些论文、综述和期刊，指出“人从任务 A 切换到任务 B 时，即使是先知道需要切换，反应速度通常仍会下降，错误率往往上升”，其背后涉及两种过程：

- Task-set Reconfiguration（任务集重构）：大脑需要重新配置目标、规则及相关信息
- Task-set Inertia（任务集惯性）：上一任务的认知不会立即消失，可能干扰新任务。

简单来讲就是，切换任务的时候并不只是简单换了一个关注对象，还涉及“解绑-重新绑定-处理竞争”，这个过程在我们实际体验上可能就是切换个窗口，脑子很快从上一个任务切换到下一个任务，但实际大脑在不知不觉间处理了一些复杂的事情。

比如“开冰箱”这件事，很简单对吧，但要教会一个两岁儿童，你会发现“开冰箱”没那么简单，因为冰箱门有吸力，你在开的时候，肌肉记忆很自然的帮你处理了“先用一个比较大的力拉开 - 打开的瞬间判断门开了 - 快速卸力并判断卸多少 - 稳定力量缓缓拉开”，这个流程涉及对力量的掌控、对物理反馈的判断、对开合大小的预期和执行等背后的细节。

所以非常能理解机器人跑步比赛为什么一个个地扑街和撞墙: D

回到 vibe coding 上来，对 AI 开发工作而言，这个现象尤其明显。例如让几个 agent 同时开工，可能会是这样：

| Agent | 当前任务        | 你需要恢复的上下文           |
| ----- | --------------- | ---------------------------- |
| A     | 修复 UI 组件    | 布局、状态、样式             |
| B     | 调研 Agent 框架 | 方案、指标、依据             |
| C     | 产品预发布      | 品牌定位、视觉语言、设计约束 |

Agent 可以同时执行，但你阅读、审查和决策时，仍然需要进入不同的任务语境，上下文管理不止对于模型很重要，对于大脑也很重要。

除了切换时的注意力损耗，切换之后还有一些隐性的消耗，你看似投入到另一个任务中了，但实际上大脑对于上一个任务的上下文清理并不彻底，还有一些注意力残留，这可能比单纯的任务切换成本更能解释我感受到的疲惫。

一个显著特征就是我会时不时地看一下刚才 session 的任务状态，不是切过去，是看看 tab 上的状态是“转圈”还是“绿点”，我会不经意地惦记其它任务，这种“吃着碗里的看着锅里的”状态也是很耗神的。

Sophie Leroy 在 2009 年提出并实验研究了 Attention Residue，核心发现是**当一个人从尚未完成的任务切换到新任务时，一部分注意力仍停留在旧任务上，从而降低新任务中的表现**。

09 年的研究肯定不是基于驾驭多个 agent 进行的，但道理相通，并且在 AI 时代这个现象反而被放大和普及了。

过去亲自开发一个功能，可能需要几个小时或几天，虽然任务难，但大部分时间都围绕同一个问题思考。现在只需要五分钟把任务交给 Agent，就可以开始另一个任务，但交出去的任务不等于在心理上结束的任务。

![](https://assets.arieszhou.com/Screenshot%202026-11-21%20at%2018-30-38.jpg)

任务在计算机中是异步执行的，在大脑中却不一定能完全异步卸载。这就形成了大量未关闭的认知任务，有任务意味着有消耗。AI 产生信息太快了，我们的理解、判断和验收能力有点跟不上，这对于认知来说属于多维度的持续压力，骆驼身上的稻草堆积的又快又多，自然很容易感到疲惫😫。

# 关于前额叶

回到文章标题，本来想用“疲惫的脑门子”，实属是才疏学浅、文笔拙劣，本着直抒胸臆的态度，我确实是感觉脑门紧所以并没有认为这个命名有什么问题，但 GPT 从神经科学和代谢的角度给我分析之后，表示其实是「前额叶」的代谢变化与疲劳表现，呈现在表面上就是头皮紧张，并建议我使用“疲惫的前额叶”作为标题，有专家建议并且这个建议更显的高大上，我自然是欣然采纳。

关于论证和分析的过程与依据，有太多专有名词很难理解，经过两轮明确要求用它浅显易懂、措辞明确的沟通方式进行友好交流后，我理解下来是这样的意思：前额叶皮层与工作记忆、目标维持、执行控制等功能密切相关，持续高认知控制需求的任务，可能伴随特定前额叶区域的代谢变化和疲劳表现。

任务切换成本、信息处理压力、持续认知控制、机制维护与恢复不足，共同导致脑力过劳，感到疲惫。

所以压力的来源不是单一某个维度的，比较有效的办法不是避免所有高强度负荷，而是提高负荷与恢复的匹配程度，并且在衡量匹配时，考虑到曾经没有注意到过的注意力消耗，留出余地，别总想着榨干自己。

与羽毛球同理，运动员能获得好的表现，靠的不是始终维持较低心率或避免剧烈波动，而是采取更经济的技战术、强度分配与即使恢复。

想要改善认知压力，需要区分：

- 有价值的高强度思考，与不必要的认知切换；
- 主动选择的专注，与被 Agent 通知牵引的被动响应；
- 真正的休息，与只是从一个任务切换到另一个任务；

以及参考番茄钟等注意力管理方法最初要解决的问题：**为持续注意力提供边界**。

我高高兴兴地冲进了 AI 布置的高并发陷阱，让我有能力同时开始更多工作，却也使我失去了这种边界。

接下来要做的事情就是：降低认知负荷，调整工作节奏，给自己恢复的时间。

# 最后

我，我今年读过的很多书、博客、newsletter，以及听过的播客，很多地方都产生过关于“AI 为什么没有让我更轻松”的困惑与探讨。或许问题并不是 AI 没有提高效率，而是效率提升之后，我们很快用更多任务填满了释放出来的空间。

我们害怕自己错过这阵风，我们焦虑自己没有大成果，我们变成了过去吐槽过的压榨打工人的资本家（屁股决定脑袋），但我们戏称自己在压榨 Agent，但只有在一次累的不行或一次生病之后，才会意识到我们在压榨自己。

过去，我们经常思考如何让机器执行得更快；现在，也许应该开始思考怎样让机器更少打扰和挤占我们。这不只是个人时间管理问题，AI 可以不知疲倦地执行任务，但人不行。

当机器的执行力不再是主要瓶颈，我们或许需要重新学习的，不是如何同时做更多事情和更快地做事情，而是如何保护和经济有效地分配自己有限的注意力。

别着急，慢慢来，Agent 的长程任务以小时记，但人的长程任务以月/年记，希望你能好好休息❤️。

# 参考资料

- 啰里八嗦的 ChatGPT
- Monsell（2003）：Task Switching
- Leroy（2009）：Attention Residue
- Wiehler et al.（2022）：认知控制与神经代谢
- 2025–2026 年关于认知疲劳机制的综述及相关研究
- 2026 年关于 AI 工作强化或 AI Brain Fry 的实证调查

午休的时候我就在琢磨这件事，偶然联想到打球，或许思考时的大脑就像运动时的身体，持续而稳定的负荷，相较于频繁启停变换，会造成额外的消耗，就像跑步和打羽毛球的区别。一个人同样的体力，跑步能坚持半个小时，但羽毛球或许十分钟就得歇一歇。

在羽毛球比赛中，业余和职业的体能差距很大，一部分原因就是职业运动员更善于采用经济的跑动步伐、合理的节奏和高效的回合间休息。那么类比多任务工作时的疲惫感，是不是因为我们在用一种很不经济的方式使用自己的大脑，或者更精确一点说是使用自己的注意力？

于是咨询了一下 GPT，简要描述了我的感受和猜想，让它分析问题的原因是否如我所想，并查查有没有类似的理论依据支撑。得到的答复很长，粗略翻一下估计得有八九页，核心观点是——**疲惫不一定来自能量被大量消耗，可能来自持续认知控制所付出的额外代价**。

理论依据引用了一些论文、综述和期刊，指出“人从任务 A 切换到任务 B 时，即使是先知道需要切换，反应速度通常仍会下降，错误率往往上升”，其背后涉及两种过程：

- Task-set Reconfiguration（任务集重构）：大脑需要重新配置目标、规则及相关信息
- Task-set Inertia（任务集惯性）：上一任务的认知不会立即消失，可能干扰新任务。

简单来讲就是，切换任务的时候并不只是简单换了一个关注对象，还涉及“解绑-重新绑定-处理竞争”，这个过程在我们实际体验上可能就是切换个窗口，脑子很快从上一个任务切换到下一个任务，但实际大脑在不知不觉间处理了一些复杂的事情。

比如“开冰箱”这件事，很简单对吧，但要教会一个两岁儿童，你会发现“开冰箱”没那么简单，因为冰箱门有吸力，你在开的时候，肌肉记忆很自然的帮你处理了“先用一个比较大的力拉开 - 打开的瞬间判断门开了 - 快速卸力并判断卸多少 - 稳定力量缓缓拉开”，这个流程涉及对力量的掌控、对物理反馈的判断、对开合大小的预期和执行等背后的细节。

所以非常能理解机器人跑步比赛为什么一个个地扑街和撞墙: D

回到 vibe coding 上来，对 AI 开发工作而言，这个现象尤其明显。例如让几个 agent 同时开工，可能会是这样：

| Agent | 当前任务        | 你需要恢复的上下文           |
| ----- | --------------- | ---------------------------- |
| A     | 修复 UI 组件    | 布局、状态、样式             |
| B     | 调研 Agent 框架 | 方案、指标、依据             |
| C     | 产品预发布      | 品牌定位、视觉语言、设计约束 |

Agent 可以同时执行，但你阅读、审查和决策时，仍然需要进入不同的任务语境，上下文管理不止对于模型很重要，对于大脑也很重要。

除了切换时的注意力损耗，切换之后还有一些隐性的消耗，你看似投入到另一个任务中了，但实际上大脑对于上一个任务的上下文清理并不彻底，还有一些注意力残留，这可能比单纯的任务切换成本更能解释我感受到的疲惫。

一个显著特征就是我会时不时地看一下刚才 session 的任务状态，不是切过去，是看看 tab 上的状态是“转圈”还是“绿点”，我会不经意地惦记其它任务，这种“吃着碗里的看着锅里的”状态也是很耗神的。

Sophie Leroy 在 2009 年提出并实验研究了 Attention Residue，核心发现是**当一个人从尚未完成的任务切换到新任务时，一部分注意力仍停留在旧任务上，从而降低新任务中的表现**。

09 年的研究肯定不是基于驾驭多个 agent 进行的，但道理相通，并且在 AI 时代这个现象反而被放大和普及了。

过去亲自开发一个功能，可能需要几个小时或几天，虽然任务难，但大部分时间都围绕同一个问题思考。现在只需要五分钟把任务交给 Agent，就可以开始另一个任务，但交出去的任务不等于在心理上结束的任务。

![](https://assets.arieszhou.com/Screenshot%202026-11-21%20at%2018-30-38.jpg)

任务在计算机中是异步执行的，在大脑中却不一定能完全异步卸载。这就形成了大量未关闭的认知任务，有任务意味着有消耗。AI 产生信息太快了，我们的理解、判断和验收能力有点跟不上，这对于认知来说属于多维度的持续压力，骆驼身上的稻草堆积的又快又多，自然很容易感到疲惫😫。

# 关于前额叶

回到文章标题，本来想用“疲惫的脑门子”，实属是才疏学浅、文笔拙劣，本着直抒胸臆的态度，我确实是感觉脑门紧所以并没有认为这个命名有什么问题，但 GPT 从神经科学和代谢的角度给我分析之后，表示其实是「前额叶」的代谢变化与疲劳表现，呈现在表面上就是头皮紧张，并建议我使用“疲惫的前额叶”作为标题，有专家建议并且这个建议更显的高大上，我自然是欣然采纳。

关于论证和分析的过程与依据，有太多专有名词很难理解，经过两轮明确要求用它浅显易懂、措辞明确的沟通方式进行友好交流后，我理解下来是这样的意思：前额叶皮层与工作记忆、目标维持、执行控制等功能密切相关，持续高认知控制需求的任务，可能伴随特定前额叶区域的代谢变化和疲劳表现。

任务切换成本、信息处理压力、持续认知控制、机制维护与恢复不足，共同导致脑力过劳，感到疲惫。

所以压力的来源不是单一某个维度的，比较有效的办法不是避免所有高强度负荷，而是提高负荷与恢复的匹配程度，并且在衡量匹配时，考虑到曾经没有注意到过的注意力消耗，留出余地，别总想着榨干自己。

与羽毛球同理，运动员能获得好的表现，靠的不是始终维持较低心率或避免剧烈波动，而是采取更经济的技战术、强度分配与即使恢复。

想要改善认知压力，需要区分：

- 有价值的高强度思考，与不必要的认知切换；
- 主动选择的专注，与被 Agent 通知牵引的被动响应；
- 真正的休息，与只是从一个任务切换到另一个任务；

以及参考番茄钟等注意力管理方法最初要解决的问题：**为持续注意力提供边界**。

我高高兴兴地冲进了 AI 布置的高并发陷阱，让我有能力同时开始更多工作，却也使我失去了这种边界。

接下来要做的事情就是：降低认知负荷，调整工作节奏，给自己恢复的时间。

# 最后

我，我今年读过的很多书、博客、newsletter，以及听过的播客，很多地方都产生过关于“AI 为什么没有让我更轻松”的困惑与探讨。或许问题并不是 AI 没有提高效率，而是效率提升之后，我们很快用更多任务填满了释放出来的空间。

我们害怕自己错过这阵风，我们焦虑自己没有大成果，我们变成了过去吐槽过的压榨打工人的资本家（屁股决定脑袋），但我们戏称自己在压榨 Agent，但只有在一次累的不行或一次生病之后，才会意识到我们在压榨自己。

过去，我们经常思考如何让机器执行得更快；现在，也许应该开始思考怎样让机器更少打扰和挤占我们。这不只是个人时间管理问题，AI 可以不知疲倦地执行任务，但人不行。

当机器的执行力不再是主要瓶颈，我们或许需要重新学习的，不是如何同时做更多事情和更快地做事情，而是如何保护和经济有效地分配自己有限的注意力。

别着急，慢慢来，Agent 的长程任务以小时记，但人的长程任务以月/年记，希望你能好好休息❤️。

# 参考资料

- 啰里八嗦的 ChatGPT
- Monsell（2003）：Task Switching
- Leroy（2009）：Attention Residue
- Wiehler et al.（2022）：认知控制与神经代谢
- 2025–2026 年关于认知疲劳机制的综述及相关研究
- 2026 年关于 AI 工作强化或 AI Brain Fry 的实证调查

我们害怕自己错过这阵风，我们焦虑自己没有大成果，我们变成了过去吐槽过的压榨打工人的资本家（屁股决定脑袋），但我们戏称自己在压榨 Agent，但只有在一次累的不行或一次生病之后，才会意识到我们在压榨自己。

过去，我们经常思考如何让机器执行得更快；现在，也许应该开始思考怎样让机器更少打扰和挤占我们。这不只是个人时间管理问题，AI 可以不知疲倦地执行任务，但人不行。

当机器的执行力不再是主要瓶颈，我们或许需要重新学习的，不是如何同时做更多事情和更快地做事情，而是如何保护和经济有效地分配自己有限的注意力。

别着急，慢慢来，Agent 的长程任务以小时记，但人的长程任务以月/年记，希望你能好好休息❤️。

参考资料

  • 啰里八嗦的 ChatGPT
  • Monsell（2003）：Task Switching
  • Leroy（2009）：Attention Residue
  • Wiehler et al.（2022）：认知控制与神经代谢
  • 2025–2026 年关于认知疲劳机制的综述及相关研究
  • 2026 年关于 AI 工作强化或 AI Brain Fry 的实证调查

title: codeyam
summary: A free creative suite, built in Rust, for AI collaboration

extra.author: nadis
extra.original_title: Show HN: A free creative suite, built in Rust, for AI collaboration

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Nadia, one of the makers of CadYam. My cofounder Jared is here to answer questions as well.

CadYam is a desktop design app built for a person and an AI agent to work on the same project: a CAD drawing, a video, an interior design plan, a data analysis, etc. You can sketch something by asking it to your agent and drop a pin on a specific place to ask for changes.

We built this after a lot of frustration trying to learn traditional CAD tools, which have a steep learning curve and take a lot of time and effort before you can build anything complex. With CadYam, the agent can do the work for you with your guidance or teach you how to use the app if you'd like to do some manual work yourself, so you also don't always need the agent.

The agent's changes show up as a preview you iterate on with natural language. No technical skills required to use it. You can watch a short demo (under a minute) at https://youtu.be/NbA28Pshxyo or click around some demo exports in your browser without installing anything: https://codeyam-ai.github.io/cadyam-exports/

We were also inspired by the HN threads about creative tools rebuilt in Rust, e.g. discussed in this HN thread: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49959605

Some technical details:

- CadYam is written in Rust and runs a local MCP server. Agents connect to it and use the same commands you do, so they can drive almost everything in the app. CadYam has instructions for connecting a range of agents.

- We built CadYam with CodeYam (codeyam.com), a product we developed for building software with AI. It lets us develop quickly while keeping the app well organized and well tested. We're shipping about two dozen fixes and features a day (more than 600 in the last month), so feature suggestions and bug reports are welcome and should get fixed quickly.

- The app is currently free for macOS, Windows, and Linux. It probably won't be free forever, but if we do charge, it will be a small amount. It's inexpensive for us to develop, and it doubles as a demo of what you can build with CodeYam.

We'd love for you to try it and share your feedback.

extra.author: mrroryflint

story_text.value:
A little while ago I built (vibed) a tiny Mac app to block websites via the hosts file. By default it imported some fairly popular adult filtering lists as well as social media etc.

It has been very effective; it would only take a few moments to switch off but it is enough of an interruption to often make me re-evaluate and proceed on.

I have a particular distain for current affairs and have found "the news" addictive for years, clearly at the detriment to my own mental health and sanity.

So, in a similar vein to the other lists I found, I have created a fairly comprehensive list of news sites that can be imported/used as you see fit.

To state the obvious, the absolute vast majority of the work was done via Claude and a small army of sub-agents.

title: Hermit CRM
summary: Free open-source CRM for solopreneurs

extra.author: gijsbos
extra.original_title: Show HN: Hermit CRM – Free open-source CRM for solopreneurs

story_text.value:
I was about to keep track of my clients and prospecting in Google Sheets for my solopreneur business, when I remembered that's exactly what I advise my clients not to do.

Created Hermit CRM, an open source CRM for 1 person. Hermit helps to keep track of deals and prospecting. The platform is built for AI by storing the data in Markdown files in git, stored locally and can be accessed with a web app, CLI or MCP. No telemetry on the app. Building in public, even the website stats are public as well.

It’s macOS first. Linux is less tested, and Windows isn’t supported.

Features I'm proud of: - import somebody from LinkedIn into to the CRM with 1 click - adding a LinkedIn convo to the CRM with 1 click. Both work without LinkedIn or CRM subs.

Don't like what you see? Fork the Hermit with your AI.

Would love to learn how you're using Hermit and where it doesn't fit your workflows.

We have a Getting Started guide for new users, and a Migration guide for anyone coming from Hammerspoon 1.

It's a beta, so expect some rough edges. Please report bugs and feature requests on GitHub.

- Vaults under ruined towers

- Autosave plus three manual slots

- No runtime dependencies

Limitations:

- Story inconsistencies

- Mismatches between story/description and visual state

- I'm sure plenty more

title: id6788552553
summary: I wrote FlightTrack twice

extra.author: bkazez
extra.original_title: Show HN: I wrote FlightTrack twice

story_text.value:
FlightTrack was my iPhone flight tracker from the early App Store days (bestselling travel app for 4 years), and I just rewrote it from scratch.

I first wrote FlightTrack as a side project in 2008. It did really well and I quit my day job and started a company around it that was bought by Expedia in 2010; Expedia retired the app in 2017. By then I had burned out and focused my energy on classical singing, which turns out to mean living in airports. But I missed the app.

This summer I started rebuilding it from scratch, with a design inspired by Paul Mijksenaar's fantastic signage at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, and working with Claude to write a server in Go and an iOS app in Swift. In 2008 v1.0 took me 6 weeks of evenings/weekends; now it took about the same amount of time, but thanks to Claude, I ended up with much more functionality (e.g. inbound flight tracking) and was able to try entire design iterations as functional code rather than just mockups.

The data is way more expensive now, so it’s a $59.99/yr subscription, but I’m giving a free year to the first 100 subscribers. I'll be adding lots of features soon but wanted to get this version out for Thanksgiving travel. Let me know anything you want and I'll do my best!

title: Taskless
summary: turn AGENTS.md and PR comments into runnable checks

extra.author: codedrift_
extra.original_title: Show HN: Taskless, turn AGENTS.md and PR comments into runnable checks

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I'm Jakob, the solo dev and founder behind Taskless.

I got tired of my AGENTS.md files being ignored or forgotten a half dozen turns into conversations. I also remembered reading someone here on HN saying we weren't using nearly enough syntax trees in our code checks. This is the result.

Taskless gives you powerful syntax tree tools with human verifiable fixtures. The CLI is MIT licensed, so running the CLI, onboarding, rule writing, and running the underlying ast-grep & Vale checks are all local. You can give it a try with:

npx @taskless/cli

and then asking your agent to "onboard with Taskless".

Under the hood, the CLI works with your agent to read your PR review comments, fixup commits, and agent files. It takes things that keep recurring and turns them into the simplest code-level enforcement that can prevent the issue going forward. By choosing code over an LLM for the runtime, there's no model once code is generated. The checks can then be committed to your codebase and enforced. I'm particularly proud of how determinism is mixed into the onboarding flow. Any time the CLI can give the agent information without letting the agent wandering the codebase, the CLI does. It results in a more consistent experience with far fewer errors. Anonymous telemetry can be disabled outright by setting DO_NOT_TRACK=1 or TASKLESS_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 in your environment (it collects CLI version, OS, the repo's org/owner, and a bit about the repository it's running in).

When the agent's done, it creates a report you can share around to show everyone there's a better way to control the output of agentic coding tools. I thought I'd include a few here from some of my favorite repos.

- Effect: https://tskl.es/gh/Effect-TS/effect/20261104/1g4gRoMmoADlysg... I specifically liked Effect because effect-bot is in the PRs fixing bugs and writing docs for the team, and they already use oxlint plugins and a TypeScript language service plugin.

- Sentry: https://tskl.es/gh/getsentry/sentry/20261016/1ZyMPva1BzaHaa5... Sentry's all open source, and David Cramer's tweeted a lot about determinism, especially now that the team is using Junior to ship code via Slack chat.

- n8n: https://tskl.es/gh/n8n-io/n8n/20261026/1C3I3yVjFyfxNFEpl4qFA... n8n has more AI driven code than the other two repos and is a good example of how bad it can get when the determinism isn't in place. Since agents tend to copy what they see from related files, problems propagate quickly.

I'd love to hear what you're doing today to keep agents behaving, or if you do kick the tires, I'd love the honest feedback.

title: NariQ
summary: BF16-level Qwen3.8-27B in a 10 GB file

extra.author: toebee
extra.original_title: NariQ: BF16-level Qwen3.8-27B in a 10 GB file

story_text.value:
We built NariQ: 3-bit-or-lower quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B that retain near-BF16 quality across agentic tasks, math, multilingual reasoning, and image understanding.

To our knowledge, this is the first 3-bit-or-lower quantization that retains BF16 lvl performance on long-horizon agentic tasks.

Benchmarks (BF16 / 3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit):

- DeepSWE: 39.8 / 41.0 / 41.9 / 28.6

- Terminal-Bench 2.1: 62.6 / 63.8 / 60.2 / 52.4

- AIME 25+26: 97.7 / 98.3 / 96.5 / 86.0

- MSGM: 94.0 / 93.1 / 91.8 / 90.6

- RealWorldQA: 82.4 / 82.4 / 81.3 / 80.9

Decode speed is comparable to other quants on an RTX PRO 6000. Context-length results below

(3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit / Unsloth UD-IQ3_XXS):

- 4K: 88.9 / 99.2 / 111.7 / 94.7

- 16K: 84.5 / 93.8 / 105.1 / 89.8

- 64K: 70.7 / 77.5 / 85.0 / 74.8

Running these currently require our llama.cpp fork: (https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp)

Feedback and questions welcome. We'd love to hear how these perform on your workloads.
